"authors": "Masanari Kimura, Takuma Nakamura, Yuki Saito",
      "url": "https://api.semanticscholar.org/CorpusId:257405224",
      "relevance": 1,
      "abstract": "Set-to-set matching is the problem of matching two different sets of items based on some criteria. Especially when each item in the set is high-dimensional, such as an image, set-to-set matching is treated as one of the applied problems to be solved by utilizing neural networks. Most machine learning-based set-to-set matching generally assumes that the training and test data follow the same distribution. However, such assumptions are often violated in real-world machine learning problems. In this paper, we propose SHIFT15M, a dataset that can be used to properly evaluate set-to-set matching models in situations where the distribution of data changes between training and testing. Some benchmark experiments show that the performance of naive methods drops due to the effects of the distribution shift. In addition, we provide software to handle SHIFT15M dataset in a very simple way: https://github.com/st-tech/zozo-shift15m. The URL for the software will appear after this manuscript is published.",
      "citations": 3
    },
    {
      "title": "Recovering Petaflops in Contrastive Semi-Supervised Learning of Visual Representations",
      "year": 2020,
      "authors": "Mahmoud Assran, Nicolas Ballas, Llu\u00eds Castrej\u00f3n, Michael G. Rabbat",
      "url": "https://api.semanticscholar.org/CorpusId:219956134",
      "relevance": 1,
      "abstract": "We investigate a strategy for improving the computational efficiency of contrastive learning of visual representations by leveraging a small amount of supervised information during pre-training. We propose a semi-supervised loss, SuNCEt, based on noise-contrastive estimation, that aims to distinguish examples of different classes in addition to the self-supervised instance-wise pretext tasks. We find that SuNCEt can be used to match the semi-supervised learning accuracy of previous contrastive approaches with significantly less computational effort. Our main insight is that leveraging even a small amount of labeled data during pre-training, and not only during fine-tuning, provides an important signal that can significantly accelerate contrastive learning of visual representations.",
      "citations": 3
    },
    {
      "title": "Winning Prize Comes from Losing Tickets: Improve Invariant Learning by Exploring Variant Parameters for Out-of-Distribution Generalization",
      "year": 2023,
      "authors": "Zhuo Huang, Muyang Li, Li Shen, Jun Yu, Chen Gong, Bo Han, Tongliang Liu",
      "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/1c6a809ca31769107f6b756b25ab6944af1fede7",
      "relevance": 1,
      "abstract": "Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Generalization aims to learn robust models that generalize well to various environments without fitting to distribution-specific features. Recent studies based on Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) address this problem by minimizing the learning target to find some of the parameters that are critical to the task. However, in open-world visual recognition problems, such solutions are suboptimal as the learning task contains severe distribution noises, which can mislead the optimization process. Therefore, apart from finding the task-related parameters (i.e., invariant parameters), we propose Exploring Variant parameters for Invariant Learning (EVIL) which also leverages the distribution knowledge to find the parameters that are sensitive to distribution shift (i.e., variant parameters). Once the variant parameters are left out of invariant learning, a robust subnetwork that is resistant to distribution shift can be found. Additionally, the parameters that are relatively stable across distributions can be considered invariant ones to improve invariant learning. By fully exploring both variant and invariant parameters, our EVIL can effectively identify a robust subnetwork to improve OOD generalization. In extensive experiments on integrated testbed: DomainBed, EVIL can effectively and efficiently enhance many popular methods, such as ERM, IRM, SAM, etc. Our code is available at https://github.com/tmllab/EVIL.",
      "citations": 19
    },
    {
      "title": "FOOGD: Federated Collaboration for Both Out-of-distribution Generalization and Detection",
      "year": 2024,
      "authors": "Xinting Liao, Weiming Liu, Pengyang Zhou, Fengyuan Yu, Jiahe Xu, Jun Wang, Wenjie Wang, Chaochao Chen, Xiaolin Zheng",
      "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/4a93e33a4e3776c4d24a92de4cdb2804c14a206c",
      "relevance": 1,
      "abstract": "Federated learning (FL) is a promising machine learning paradigm that collaborates with client models to capture global knowledge. However, deploying FL models in real-world scenarios remains unreliable due to the coexistence of in-distribution data and unexpected out-of-distribution (OOD) data, such as covariate-shift and semantic-shift data. Current FL researches typically address either covariate-shift data through OOD generalization or semantic-shift data via OOD detection, overlooking the simultaneous occurrence of various OOD shifts. In this work, we propose FOOGD, a method that estimates the probability density of each client and obtains reliable global distribution as guidance for the subsequent FL process. Firstly, SM3D in FOOGD estimates score model for arbitrary distributions without prior constraints, and detects semantic-shift data powerfully. Then SAG in FOOGD provides invariant yet diverse knowledge for both local covariate-shift generalization and client performance generalization. In empirical validations, FOOGD significantly enjoys three main advantages: (1) reliably estimating non-normalized decentralized distributions, (2) detecting semantic shift data via score values, and (3) generalizing to covariate-shift data by regularizing feature extractor. The prejoct is open in https://github.com/XeniaLLL/FOOGD-main.git.",
      "citations": 16
    },
    {
      "title": "Online test-time adaptation for better generalization of interatomic potentials to out-of-distribution data",
      "year": 2025,
      "authors": "Taoyong Cui, Chenyu Tang, Dongzhan Zhou, Yuqiang Li, Xingao Gong, Wanli Ouyang, Mao Su, Shufei Zhang",
      "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/b321649c55a0f47ef964a1eeaefe5b2d2ac81abb",
      "relevance": 1,
      "abstract": "Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) enable more efficient molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with ab initio accuracy, which have been used in various domains of physical science. However, distribution shift between training and test data causes deterioration of the test performance of MLIPs, and even leads to collapse of MD simulations. In this work, we propose an online Test-time Adaptation Interatomic Potential (TAIP) framework to improve the generalization on test data. Specifically, we design a dual-level self-supervised learning approach that leverages global structure and atomic local environment information to align the model with the test data. Extensive experiments demonstrate TAIP\u2019s capability to bridge the domain gap between training and test dataset without additional data. TAIP enhances the test performance on various benchmarks, from small molecule datasets to complex periodic molecular systems with various types of elements. TAIP also enables stable MD simulations where the corresponding baseline models collapse. Molecular dynamics simulations using machine learning interatomic potentials often face stability issues due to distribution shifts. Here, the authors develop an online test-time adaptation framework to improve generalization, allowing for more stable simulations without the need for additional training data.",
      "citations": 13
    },
    {
      "title": "Bridging Multicalibration and Out-of-distribution Generalization Beyond Covariate Shift",
      "year": 2024,
      "authors": "Jiayun Wu, Jiashuo Liu, Peng Cui, Zhiwei Steven Wu",
      "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/03dd209a79b302cd7bc976c0bbe6761c152c05b3",
      "relevance": 1,
      "abstract": "We establish a new model-agnostic optimization framework for out-of-distribution generalization via multicalibration, a criterion that ensures a predictor is calibrated across a family of overlapping groups. Multicalibration is shown to be associated with robustness of statistical inference under covariate shift. We further establish a link between multicalibration and robustness for prediction tasks both under and beyond covariate shift. We accomplish this by extending multicalibration to incorporate grouping functions that consider covariates and labels jointly. This leads to an equivalence of the extended multicalibration and invariance, an objective for robust learning in existence of concept shift. We show a linear structure of the grouping function class spanned by density ratios, resulting in a unifying framework for robust learning by designing specific grouping functions. We propose MC-Pseudolabel, a post-processing algorithm to achieve both extended multicalibration and out-of-distribution generalization. The algorithm, with lightweight hyperparameters and optimization through a series of supervised regression steps, achieves superior performance on real-world datasets with distribution shift.",
      "citations": 12
    },
    {
      "title": "Improving Generalization of Dynamic Graph Learning via Environment Prompt",
      "year": 2024,
      "authors": "Kuo Yang, Zhen-Qiang Zhou, Qihe Huang, Limin Li, Yuxuan Liang, Yang Wang",
      "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/cb6ebbfd436f110a19bc88975222230d84a7c54a",
      "relevance": 1,
      "abstract": "Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization issue is a well-known challenge within deep learning tasks. In dynamic graphs, the change of temporal environments is regarded as the main cause of data distribution shift. While numerous OOD studies focusing on environment factors have achieved remarkable performance, they still fail to systematically solve the two issue of environment inference and utilization. In this work, we propose a novel dynamic graph learning model named EpoD based on prompt learning and structural causal model to comprehensively enhance both environment inference and utilization. Inspired by the superior performance of prompt learning in understanding underlying semantic and causal associations, we \ufb01rst design a self-prompted learning mechanism to infer unseen environment factors. We then rethink the role of environment variable within spatio-temporal causal structure model, and introduce a novel causal pathway where dynamic sub-graphs serve as mediating variables. The extracted dynamic subgraph can effectively capture the data distribution shift by incorporating the inferred environment variables into the node-wise dependencies. Theoretical discussions and intuitive analysis support the generalizability and interpretability of EpoD. import json
results = {}
import glob
for f in glob.glob('paper_search_results/*.jsonl'):

            try:

                key = paper.get('title','').strip()
                if key and key not in results:
                    results[key] = paper
            except: pass
# Sort by relevance then citations
papers = sorted(results.values(), key=lambda x: (-x.get('relevance',0), -x.get('citations',0)))
for p in papers[:40]:
    rel = p.get('relevance',0)
    cit = p.get('citations',0)
    yr = p.get('year','?')
    url = p.get('url','')
    print(f'[R{rel} C{cit}] ({yr}) {p[\"title\"][:80]}')
    print(f'  {url}')
"

import json, glob

results = {}
for f in glob.glob('paper_search_results/*.jsonl'):
    with open(f) as fh:
        for line in fh:
            try:
                paper = json.loads(line)
                key = paper.get('title','').strip()
                if key and key not in results:
                    results[key] = paper
            except: pass

# Key papers for our hypothesis - most directly relevant
# Focus: curriculum learning for LLMs, distribution shift in pretraining, domain generalization
priority_keywords = [
    'curriculum', 'pre-train', 'pretrain', 'language model',
    'data ordering', 'distribution shift', 'domain general',
    'invariant risk', 'distributionally robust', 'group shift'
]

papers = sorted(results.values(), key=lambda x: (-x.get('relevance',0), -x.get('citations',0)))

# Score papers by keyword match
scored = []
for p in papers:
    if p.get('relevance', 0) < 2:
        continue
    title_lower = p.get('title','').lower()
    abstract_lower = p.get('abstract','').lower()
    kw_score = sum(1 for kw in priority_keywords if kw in title_lower or kw in abstract_lower)
    scored.append((kw_score, p))

scored.sort(key=lambda x: (-x[0], -x[1].get('relevance',0), -x[1].get('citations',0)))

# Print top 30 most relevant
for kw_score, p in scored[:30]:
    rel = p.get('relevance',0)
    cit = p.get('citations',0)
    yr = p.get('year','?')
    print(f'[KW{kw_score} R{rel} C{cit}] ({yr}) {p["title"][:80]}')
    # Extract arxiv ID if present
    url = p.get('url','')
    print(f'  URL: {url}')
PYEOF

import requests, json, time, os, re

with open('papers/key_papers.json') as f:
    papers = json.load(f)

# Deduplicate by title
seen = set()
unique = []
for p in papers:
    t = p['title'].strip().lower()
    if t not in seen:
        seen.add(t)
        unique.append(p)

print(f"Unique papers to download: {len(unique)}")

# Try to resolve Semantic Scholar URLs to arxiv IDs
def get_arxiv_id_from_s2(url):
    """Extract paper ID and query S2 API for arxiv ID"""
    # Extract paper ID or corpus ID
    m = re.search(r'/paper/([a-f0-9]+)', url)
    corpus_m = re.search(r'CorpusId:(\d+)', url)
    
    if m:
        pid = m.group(1)
        api_url = f"https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/{pid}?fields=externalIds"
    elif corpus_m:
        cid = corpus_m.group(1)
        api_url = f"https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/CorpusID:{cid}?fields=externalIds"
    else:
        return None
    
    try:
        r = requests.get(api_url, timeout=10)
        if r.status_code == 200:
            data = r.json()
            ext = data.get('externalIds', {})
            return ext.get('ArXiv')
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  Error: {e}")
    return None

# Resolve and download
downloaded = []
failed = []

for i, p in enumerate(unique):
    title = p['title']
    url = p.get('url', '')
    safe_title = re.sub(r'[^a-zA-Z0-9]+', '_', title)[:60].strip('_')
    
    print(f"\n[{i+1}/{len(unique)}] {title[:70]}")
    
    # Get arxiv ID
    arxiv_id = get_arxiv_id_from_s2(url)
    if arxiv_id:
        pdf_url = f"https://arxiv.org/pdf/{arxiv_id}.pdf"
        filename = f"papers/{arxiv_id}_{safe_title}.pdf"
        
        if os.path.exists(filename):
            print(f"  Already exists: {filename}")
            downloaded.append({'title': title, 'file': filename, 'arxiv_id': arxiv_id, **p})
            continue
            
        try:
            r = requests.get(pdf_url, timeout=30)
            if r.status_code == 200 and len(r.content) > 1000:
                with open(filename, 'wb') as f:
                    f.write(r.content)
                print(f"  Downloaded: {filename} ({len(r.content)//1024}KB)")
                downloaded.append({'title': title, 'file': filename, 'arxiv_id': arxiv_id, **p})
            else:
                print(f"  Failed: status={r.status_code}")
                failed.append(title)
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"  Error: {e}")
            failed.append(title)
    else:
        print(f"  No arxiv ID found")
        failed.append(title)
    
    time.sleep(0.5)  # Rate limit

print(f"\n\nDownloaded: {len(downloaded)}")
print(f"Failed: {len(failed)}")
for t in failed:
    print(f"  - {t[:70]}")

# Save download manifest
with open('papers/downloaded.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(downloaded, f, indent=2)
PYEOF

Irreducible Curriculum
for Language Model Pretraining
Simin Fan
EPFL
simin.fan@epfl.ch
Martin Jaggi
EPFL
martin.jaggi@epfl.ch
Abstract
Automatic data selection and curriculum design for training large language models
is challenging, with only a few existing methods showing improvements over
standard training. Furthermore, current schemes focus on domain-level selec-
tion, overlooking the more fine-grained contributions of each individual training
point. It is difficult to apply traditional datapoint selection methods on large lan-
guage models: most online batch selection methods perform two-times forward
or backward passes, which introduces considerable extra costs with large-scale
models. To mitigate these obstacles, we propose IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM as a
curriculum learning algorithm for language model pretraining, which prioritizes
samples with higher learnability. Specifically, to avoid prohibitive extra compu-
tation overhead, we simulate the sample loss along the main model’s training
trajectory using a small-scale proxy model. Our experiments on the RedPajama-1B
dataset demonstrate a consistent improvement on validation perplexity across all 7
domains compared to random uniform baseline and the anti-curriculum strategy.
Our method also reduces the sharpness of the network and illustrates a better 5-shot
accuracy on MMLU benchmarks.
1
Introduction
The evolution of language models demonstrates impressive generation and reasoning abilities from
a continuous scaling-up of model size and training corpus [Brown et al., 2020, Chowdhery et al.,
2022, Kaplan et al., 2020, Hoffmann et al., 2022], along with very significant growth in computation
cost. Besides the quantity [Kaplan et al., 2020] and quality [Lee et al., 2022, Longpre et al., 2023] of
training data, several recent works show that the ordering [Chen et al., 2023] and composition [Xie
et al., 2023] of data during the training can highly impact performance and efficiency. Xie et al.
[2023] proposes DOREMI, which determines the optimal domain mixture to construct the pretraining
corpus using auxiliary models; Chen et al. [2023] introduces an online selection scheme, which
seeks to dynamically update the mixture of data from each skill-set at each training step. While
DOREMI and SKILL-IT demonstrates great downstream performance, their curriculum are built upon
the group-level where all the instances within one group (domain/skill) shares the same sampling
probability, without looking inside each domains on the sample-specific attributions.
Nevertheless, few research have succeeded applying traditional sample-level selection schemes for
large langauge model pretraining. Online batch selection methods [Loshchilov and Hutter, 2015,
Katharopoulos and Fleuret, 2018, Jiang et al., 2019, Schaul et al., 2015] select hard samples with
high loss or high gradient norm, which require a second forward/backward pass. That introduces
large extra computation costs when the model size is large, which hurts the scalability. On the
other side, Campos [2021] shows that the linguistic-based curriculum learning failed to improve on
causal language model pretraining. Schaul et al. [2015] introduces RHO-LOSS, which is an online
batch selection scheme based on the gap between current training loss and an irreducible loss term

measured using a proxy model. Inspired by the idea of proxy model approximation, we propose
IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM as a curriculum learning algorithm, construct an ordered data stream
by simulating the learning trajectory of large model through the lens of a small-scale proxy model.
Specifically, we train the small-scale proxy model on a holdout set, and measure the loss on each
data samples in the training set using the proxy model at different training stages. We estimate the
learnability score of the training samples by the loss gap from the proxy model at early- and late-stage.
The IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM would prioritize the samples with highest learnability score and
proceed to the samples with lower learnability score. We present the details of our methodology in
Section 3.

Qualitatively, RHO-LOSS down-weighs the redundant, noisy samples and outliers: redundant points

3
Irreducible Curriculum
Aiming to reduce the computation cost while improving the training efficiency and robustness, we
tend to design a pre-defined curriculum to simulate the online assessment of the scores L[y|x; Dt]
along the training process. We refer to our algorithm as IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM, since it is
determined only by a proxy-model trained on a holdout dataset without resorting any large model’s
training dynamics.
Specifically, we train a small proxy model Mproxy(θ′) on holdout set Dho for T overall
steps while saving an early-stage checkpoint at t0 steps (Mproxy(θ′)[t0]) and a late-stage
checkpoint(Mproxy(θ′)[T]). We define the learnability score for every sample (x, y) ∈Dt of the
training set as the gap between the loss from early-stage and the late-stage proxy model checkpoints1:

4
Experiments and Results
In this section, we present our initial inquiry experimental results on RedPajama-1B dataset, includ-
ing 7 domains3. We randomly split each domain dataset into two subsets Dproxy and Dtrain. Dproxy
is used to train the proxy model, which is applied to score Dtrain and construct the curriculum.
Considering a severe unbalance in domain scale, we uniformly sample from each domain, while
applying our proposed IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM inside each domain. We also provide the results
applying the curriculum on the whole dataset in Section 5.
We use a 6-layer (82M) model as the proxy model Mproxy(θ′) to construct the curriculum, which is
applied to train a 12-layer (124M) model M(θ). Both the proxy model and the full size model follow
the decoder-only transformer architecture [Vaswani et al., 2023] and share the same set of training
hyperparameters (batch size 64, context length 512, learning rate 3e-4). We compare IRREDUCIBLE
CURRICULUM (CURRICULUM) with random uniformly sampling baseline (RS) and anti-curriculum
(ANTI-CURRICULUM), where we start with a fraction of λ0 samples with lowest score, and then
increase the sampling upper bound with the same rate.
4.1
Result and Analysis

Figure 1: Domain-wise Validation Log-Perplexity on RedPajama-1B. It demonstrates IRREDUCIBLE
CURRICULUM consistently outperforms BASELINE and ANTI-CURRICULUM.
IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM consistently improve downstream performance on all domains.
We apply the irreducible curriculum across every domain within the RedPajama-1B4 dataset, with
λ0 = 50%, early stage checkpoint is saved at t0 = 2000 steps. We train the proxy model (82M)
and full model (124M) for T = 10′000 steps. Since the large model would learn faster than
the proxy model, we set Tc = 5000 < T to compensate the learning pace. According to Figure 1,
IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM consistently reaches a lower validation perplexity across all 7 domains
compared with the uniformly random baseline, even trained on a relatively small dataset. Conversely,
the ANTI-CURRICULUM approach leads to a deterioration in the evaluation performance across all
domains.
We also perform experiments by varying the values of λ0 and Tc (Table 1). Notably, all the settings
applying IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM outperform the random uniform sampling baseline, except
for the case of (λ0 = 25%, Tc = 10′000). A possible explanation for this is that the step function
determined by the proxy model inadequately addresses the differing learning paces between the large
and small proxy models. On the contrary, all experiment settings in the ANTI-CURRICULUM group
yield worse validation perplexity results.
Additionally, the empirical results shows that both IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM and ANTI-
CURRICULUM approaches outperform the baseline on the 5-shot inference accuracy on MMLU
benchmark [Hendrycks et al., 2021a]. Specifically, (λ0 = 25%, Tc = 5000) works best among all the
CURRICULUM settings. Besides, it is worth noting that both CURRICULUM and ANTI-CURRICULUM
improve the reasoning capability compared to baseline, which indicates the subset which contributes
the most in perplexity not necessarily contains valuable factual knowledge. How to tackle with this
mis-alignment towards our final target could also be a future challenge.
IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM reduces sharpness during training.
Several recent research shows
that applying sharpness aware minimization could effectively improve the generalization ability of
the network [Foret et al., 2021]. Thus, we resort to inspect into how the IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM
could impact the loss landscape by estimating its sharpness along the training trajectory. Following
[Wu, 2018, Li et al., 2022b], we adopt the popular definition of sharpness as the largest eigenvalue of
the Hessian matrix. We compute the Hessian of all the dense layers and record its top-eigenvalue
every 200 steps along the training process. More details on sharpness computation are provided in
Appendix A.
According to Fig. 2, training with IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM results to a lower sharpness compared
with random baseline. On the opposite, the anti-curriculum would lead to a sharper training trajectory.
However, whether and how this lower-sharpness correlates with the generalization ability of the
network need further explorations on larger scale models and datasets.

Analysis and Failure Mode of Global Curriculum on the Data Mixture
Assuming that we have no access to the domain information during training, we can only apply the
curriculum on globally on the entire data mixture. Instead of starting with top-λ0 fraction of samples
in each domains, we rank all samples in the global dataset and start sampling from top-scored λ0
fraction, which could mostly come from one specific domain.
Here, we compare to the anti-curriculum applied on the whole data mixture, and the baseline with
uniformly sampling across all instances. The model scale, architecture, and hyperparameters are the
same as in Section 4.1.
Global curriculum lowers average validation perplexity and reduces sharpness.
According
to Fig. 3, the blue lines denote IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM with various combination of λ0 and
Tc5, while the green lines apply ANTI-CURRICULUM. Across the entire domain-mixture corpus, the

We further evaluate the domain-wise
performance with the global curriculum applied on the entire corpus. According to Fig. 5, IRRE-
DUCIBLE CURRICULUM reduce the validation perplexity on 4 domains (C4, CommonCrawl, Book
and Wikipedia), while showing the opposite effect on the other 3 domains (Arxiv, Github and Stack-
exchange). This can be explained by the domain-wise differences in the learnability score. Figure
4 shows that most of the globally top-ranked samples are from Wikipedia, C4 and CommonCrawl
domains, which would be prioritized by the IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM while instances from
Github and Stackexchange are mostly within the quarter with lowest scores, which are primarily
learnt by the ANTI-CURRICULUM algorithm. In addition, the in-domain score distributions are highly
varying among domains. It illustrates that the an intra-domain learnability (Equ. 3) ranking would
offer a more fair comparison, while the naive global curriculum could risk from introducing too much
inter-domain sampling bias.

Future work
Scaling up the model and training corpus.
Given the emergency ability of large language
models, future work is warranted to explore how this IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM can improve the
performance of larger scale models, in particular with respect to scaling laws relating dataset size and
model size.
Relation between sharpness, generalization ability and curriculum learning.
In Section 4.1, we
observed that the IRREDUCIBLE CURRICULUM could lead to a lower sharpness of the network along

the training process while the ANTI-CURRICULUM approach would lead to the opposite. According
to the recent debate on the correlation between sharpness and generalization ability of foundation

Sharpness.
Denote the hessian matrix as H, we adopt a popular definition of the sharpness as the

Related Work
Curriculum Learning for Language Modeling.
As a popular concept in education and cognitive
science, there have been plenty of attempts to apply curriculum learning on training language models,
by progressively expose the neural learner with samples with ascending difficulty level [Campos,
2021, Nagatsuka et al., 2021, Li et al., 2022a]. However, most of the effective methods increase the
difficulty by varying the context length of sequences, without focusing on the syntactic nor semantic
properties. Li et al. [2022a] empirically proves that with a incrementally increase context length, the
pretraining of language model could be more stable, reducing the number of loss spikes. Similarly,
Nagatsuka et al. [2021] shows that feed training samples with increasing block size could improve
the performance when pretraining BERT [Devlin et al., 2019], an encoder-only model with masked
language modeling objective.
Campos [2021] has conducted extensive experiments towards using linguistic-featured curriculum
learning for language model pretraining. However, the conclusion shows their curriculum fails to
effectively help with validation perplexity nor downstream performance.
Recently, Xie et al. [2023] has introduced a domain reweighting framework by sampling from
domains with various probability. They propose to use two small-scale auxiliary models to determine
the domain weights through a group distributional robust optimization game. However, all the
samples within one domain would share the same sampling weights, which fails to distinguish the
instance-wise attributes inside the domain barrier. How to combine the domain-level reweighting and
the in-domain curriculum could also be a promising direction for future exploration.

incompatibility between the ascending data quality order and the decaying learn-

outperforms random shuffling when using a constant LR, its advantage diminishes
under standard LR decay schedules. Our experiments show this incompatibility
can be mitigated by two simple strategies: (1) employing a more moderate LR
decay schedule, where the final LR is only moderately smaller than the peak LR,
and (2) replacing LR decay with model averaging, i.e., computing a weighted av-

the average score on a suite of standard benchmarks by 1.64% over random shuf-
fling, without additional data refinement. Validated on 1.5B-parameter models
trained over 30B tokens with various data-quality metrics, our findings call for a
re-evaluation of curriculum-based LLM pretraining and underscore the potential
of co-designing data curricula with optimization methods.

171	One successful curriculum learning strategy is multi-stage pretraining: first training on a data mix-
172	ture dominated by massive web data, then in the second stage, referred to as mid-training (OLMo
173	et al., 2025; Abdin et al., 2024b), shifting the data mixture to one that mainly consists of high-quality
174	data. This strategy has been adopted by many recent LLMs, including OLMo 2 (OLMo et al., 2025),
175	Phi-4 (Abdin et al., 2024a), and LongCat-Flash (Team et al., 2025). This two-phase design is most
176	common, and it is also promising to extend with more stages (Yiwen et al., 2025; Allal et al., 2025)
177	or follow with long-context extension (Yang et al., 2025).
178	Another line of work explores curriculum learning at the instance level, where data samples are
179	sorted according to quality scores and presented to the model sequentially (Wettig et al., 2024;
180	Dai et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Kim & Lee, 2024). We refer to this as the data curriculum2.
181	However, these studies mainly investigate different quality metrics and find that simple end-to-end
182	sorting yields limited benefits. Consequently, several works propose alternative strategies such as
183	folding curriculum (Detailed in Section 4), which reorders samples within consecutive phases in an
184	interleaved manner (Dai et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Despite showing promise, we find that this
185	interleaved approach is fragile: its advantage does not extend to our larger-scale experiments with
186	the DCLM fastText score (Li et al., 2024), a widely used scoring metric (see Section 4).
187	This raises a central question: Why do instance-level curriculum learning strategies often yield
188	limited benefits? This is not simply due to unreliable quality scores: metrics like the QuRating
189	score (proposed and used by Wettig et al. (2024)), the PDS score (proposed by Gu et al. (2025b)
190	and discussed by Dai et al. (2025)), and the DCLM score (Li et al., 2024) are already informative
191	enough to improve training efficiency by guiding high-quality data selection.
192	Our Contributions.
193	In this paper, we identify a key, yet previously overlooked factor: the incom-
194	patibility between the ascending order of data quality and the decaying schedule of learning rate.
195	As illustrated in Figure 1, if we train an LLM with a constant LR, using a data curriculum that sorts

202	data in ascending order of quality can indeed outperform the baseline that trains the model on data
203	in a uniform order. However, when we switch to a more standard LR decay schedule, such as cosine
204	or Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017; Hu et al., 2024) (a schedule with
205	warmup, plateau, and decay phases, see Figure 1(b)), the benefit of the data curriculum diminishes.
206	Moreover, we observe that as the LR decay becomes more aggressive (e.g., having a longer decay
207	phase or a lower ending LR), the benefit of the data curriculum diminishes more.
208	To resolve the incompatibility between data curriculum and LR decay, firstly, we discuss a straight-
209	forward remedy: adopting a moderate LR decay schedule in curriculum learning. In Section 5.1,
210	we show that tuning the ending LR in WSD schedules trades off the benefits of data curriculum and
211	loss convergence, and setting it to a moderate value (approximately decaying to 1/3 of peak LR in
212	our setting) can make use of high-quality data and outperform uniform data ordering.
213	Further, we propose a strategy that largely resolves the incompatibility between the data curriculum
214	and the LR schedule by replacing LR decay with weight averaging (Li et al., 2025c; Izmailov et al.,
215	2018; Tian et al., 2025). Weight averaging computes a weighted average of recent checkpoints as
216	the final model. It stabilizes model parameters and reduces noise in the training process, similar to
217	the effect of LR decay. However, it can achieve this without diminishing the magnitude of updates.
218	Therefore, we adopt a constant LR throughout training and pair weight averaging with the data
219	curriculum. This combination allows the model to maintain a high learning rate and fully exploit
220	the high-quality data introduced later in the curriculum. We call this approach Curriculum Model
221	Averaging (CMA). Notably, CMA also extends emerging practices of introducing weight averaging
222	into LLM training (Tian et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025c; Sanyal et al., 2024), showing that combining
223	weight averaging with curriculum learning yields greater benefits than applying weight averaging to
224	standard uniform-ordering pretraining. This combination is particularly effective under multi-phase
225	pretraining, where high-quality data is introduced in the mid-training phase. In this setting, our
226	approach achieves an average improvement of 1.2% in accuracy—and over 2% on core benchmarks
227	(defined in Section 4)—solely by reordering data samples (Table 2).
228	Building on these explorations, we further demonstrate that combining moderate LR decay, cur-
229	riculum learning, and weight averaging can produce synergistic advantages and reveal a previously
230	overlooked high-performing pretraining regime, improving standard benchmarks by 1.64% in aver-
231	age accuracy over random shuffling and standard decay. This finding underlines that hyperparam-
232	eter settings optimized for uniform data ordering are not necessarily optimal for curriculum-based
233	training. Prior work has naturally evaluated curriculum-based training using regimes originally opti-
234	mized for uniform data ordering. However, this regime is suboptimal for curriculum-based training
235	and, as previously reported, leads to only marginal benefits (Wettig et al., 2024; Kim & Lee, 2024).
236	In contrast, we identify a previously underexplored and more effective regime in the design space of
237	LLM pretraining by co-designing these components, paving the way for future exploration.
238	We validate our hypotheses and proposed strategies through experiments at a scale sufficient to
239	support our conclusions, training a 1.5 billion-parameter model on 30 billion tokens. Our findings
240	demonstrate robustness across different quality metrics, LR schedules, and data mixtures, highlight-
241	ing that co-designing data curricula with training dynamics is a powerful, data-aware strategy for
242	improving LLM pretraining efficiency.

244	RELATED WORK
245	Curriculum Learning in LLM Pretraining.
246	While data quality is known to be critical, lever-
247	aging it through fine-grained, instance-level curricula has shown limited success and has not been
248	validated at a substantial scale (Dai et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Wettig et al., 2024; Campos,
249	2021). Prior studies have reported only marginal gains, sometimes observing benefits from counter-
250	intuitive data orders without a clear underlying mechanism (Wettig et al., 2024). Other works either
251	lack sufficient validation (Campos, 2021; Kim & Lee, 2024) or, finding simple curricula ineffective,
252	propose more complex strategies like data folding (Zhang et al., 2025; Dai et al., 2025). However,
253	we find that the benefits of such complex strategies are often confined to smaller-scale experiments
254	with low learning rates and can degrade at larger scales and under a high LR regime (Section B.1).
255	A common thread in these attempts is the use of standard cosine learning rate schedules. We demon-
256	strate that decayed LR prevents the model from effectively learning from the high-quality data in-
257	troduced late in the training process, showing that a more moderate decay is required to unlock the
258	curriculum’s full potential. A more detailed discussion can refer to Section B.1.

264	Learning Rate Schedules.
265	The learning rate (LR) schedule is a crucial hyperparameter in model
266	pretraining. Traditional LR schedules like cosine decay are the most widely used in LLM pre-
267	training (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017; Dubey et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024). More recent schedules
268	like Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) have demonstrated strong performance and are suitable for mid-
269	training resumption paradigms (Hu et al., 2024; H¨agele et al., 2024). Loss curve scaling laws suggest
270	that they possess an optimal shape for a given peak LR (Tissue et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Li et al.,
271	2025a). A prevailing finding for training with standard uniform data ordering is that an optimal or
272	near-optimal LR schedule should decay to a value close to zero (Li et al., 2025b; OLMo et al., 2025;
273	Li et al., 2024). Our work challenges this convention in the context of curriculum-based pretrain-
274	ing. We find that for a data curriculum, such an aggressive decay has negative effects on the data
275	schedule. Instead, a moderate decay that maintains a higher learning rate during the high-quality
276	data phase proves superior, especially when using model averaging. Unless otherwise specified, we
277	discuss the LR schedules with a warmup phase. For example, a constant LR schedule refers to a
278	linear warmup followed by a constant LR.
279	Model Averaging.
280	Model averaging, which combines parameters from multiple checkpoints to
281	produce a final, improved model, is a well-established technique for improving generalization (Iz-
282	mailov et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024b). It has been successfully applied in LLM
283	pretraining to accelerate convergence and boost performance, and was reportedly used in training
284	prominent models like Llama 3 (Kaddour, 2022; Li et al., 2025c; Dubey et al., 2024). Prior work
285	has explored combining model averaging with decay-free LR schedules for training on uniformly
286	ordered data and in the mid-training setting (Li et al., 2025c; Tian et al., 2025). However, Li et al.
287	(2025c) finds that the performance of weight averaging is merely comparable to standard LR decay,
288	and Tian et al. (2025) attempts to improve the results through a weighting strategy derived from the
289	LR schedule (Discussed in Sections A.2 and 3). Unlike this prior work, which focused on uniform
290	data ordering, our research is the first to investigate the interaction between model averaging and a
291	quality-based data curriculum. We find that these two strategies have a strong synergistic relation-
292	ship, as model averaging provides the necessary training stability to learn from high-quality data
293	with a high, moderately decaying learning rate.

457	Data Scoring.
458	Raw web data must pass through a processing pipeline before it is used for pretrain-
459	ing. The raw data first goes through heuristic filtering rules. Then in the model-based filtering phase,
460	a scorer model assigns a quality score to each data sample. For example, DCLM Baseline dataset
461	uses scores from a fasttext model (Joulin et al., 2017) measuring similarity to high-quality sources
462	like OpenHermes 2.5 (Teknium, 2023) and top posts from the ELI5 subreddit. Another approach,
463	PreSelect (SHUM et al., 2025), scores data based on its similarity to downstream tasks. Typically,
464	these scores are used to filter the dataset by removing samples below a certain quality threshold. In
465	contrast, our work does not use these scores to discard data; instead, we use these quality scores to
466	define the data ordering for curriculum learning.

468	LEARNING RATE DECAY COUNTERACTS DATA CURRICULUM
469	In this section, we analyze the critical yet often overlooked interaction between the learning rate
470	(LR) schedule and the data schedule. We first explain how the learning rate acts as an implicit
471	importance weight for each data sample. We then present empirical results to demonstrate three
472	key points: (1) a data curriculum can yield significant benefits over a uniform data order under a
473	constant LR schedule; (2) these benefits diminish when a conventional decaying LR schedule is
474	applied, particularly during the final, high-quality data regime; and (3) while adjustments to the data
475	schedule can mitigate this issue, the underlying conflict persists.
476	Analysis of Coupling between Learning Rate and Data Schedules.
477	A key insight is that the
478	learning rate schedule acts as an implicit importance weight for each training sample. The parame-
479	ter update at training step t is θt+1 = θt −ηtgt, where ηt is the learning rate. The gradient gt can be
480	decomposed into a signal component, E[gt], which points in the direction of steady improvement,
481	and a noise component, ϵt. A decaying learning rate ηt serves a dual purpose: it reduces the noise
482	ϵt to stabilize training, but it also shrinks the update step taken in the signal direction E[gt]. While
483	modern optimizers like Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) use more complex update rules, the learning
484	rate remains a dominant factor in the update magnitude. This dual role of ηt creates a fundamental
485	conflict in quality-based curricula. High-quality samples are intentionally processed at the end of
486	training, but this is precisely when conventional LR schedules reduce ηt to its minimum. Conse-
487	quently, the decaying learning rate diminishes the influence of the most valuable data, counteracting
488	the intended benefit of the curriculum.
489	Experimental Settings.
490	Our experiments are grounded in the DataComps-LM (DCLM) frame-
491	work (Li et al., 2024) at the 1B-1x scale, ensuring our findings are validated at a substantial scale.

579	order curriculum, and a reverse (descending-order) curriculum, both curricula sorted by DCLM

587	The Curriculum’s Advantage Diminishes with a Decaying LR Schedule.
588	In sharp contrast to
589	the constant LR experiments, the advantage of the data curriculum largely disappears when we
590	employ a WSD schedule (Figure 1(b)). The performance degradation is even more pronounced with

592	relationship, we varied the aggressiveness of the LR decay by adjusting two WSD parameters: the
593	number of decay steps and the final learning rate. The results in Figure 2 show a clear trend: as
594	the decay phase becomes longer or more aggressive (i.e., a smaller ending LR), the performance
595	benefit of the data curriculum over the uniform baseline shrinks, eventually becoming negligible.
596	This confirms the previously overlooked effect of LR decay on the data curriculum, where LR decay
597	undermines the contribution of high-quality data.

768	UNLOCKING DATA CURRICULA POTENTIAL VIA MODERATE LR DECAY
769	AND MODEL AVERAGING
770	To resolve the interaction between data curricula and learning rate (LR) schedules, we first utilize
771	a more moderate LR decay in place of a standard aggressive decay, which we find mitigates the
772	issue. We then turn to a more principled approach: model averaging (Izmailov et al., 2018; Li et al.,
773	2025c; Tian et al., 2025). We investigate replacing LR decay entirely with model averaging, which
774	allows high-quality data to be processed with a constant learning rate. While model averaging alone
775	may not match the performance of LR decay with uniform data, we find that combining a data cur-
776	riculum with model averaging produces comparable or even superior results to a standard decaying
777	LR schedule, particularly in a mid-training setting. This reveals a synergistic relationship between
778	data curricula and model averaging. Furthermore, we find that a combination of model averaging
779	and moderate LR decay can yield even stronger and stable results for curriculum-based pretraining.
780	Our results highlight a previously unexplored regime for improving LLM pretraining and reveal the
781	potential of co-designing LR schedules, data curricula, and model averaging strategies.
782	5.1
783	MITIGATING NEGATIVE INTERACTION WITH MODERATE LEARNING RATE DECAY
784	A straightforward way to mitigate the negative impact of LR decay on data curricula is to use a
785	moderate LR decay instead of a standard aggressive one. As shown in Figure 2, for uniform data,
786	the validation loss decreases with more aggressive LR decay, like increasing decay steps and lower
787	ending LRs in our experimental setting. In comparison, the benefits of data curricula increase with
788	a more moderate LR decay, like fewer decay steps or higher ending LRs. The different preferences
789	of LR decay suggest that the optimal ending LR or number of decay steps can differ for curriculum-
790	based training from uniform data training, also indicated by the validation loss curves in Figure 2.
791	Since the optimal ending LR is typically close to zero for uniform data ordering, but more decay
792	steps are not always better (Li et al., 2025b; 2024; Hu et al., 2024), it is more convenient to ablate
793	on the ending LRs to see whether the optimal LR schedule changes for curricula.
794	To investigate this, we run experiments on ending LRs in a fine-grained manner and report the
795	training results for both uniform data ordering and a data curriculum. As shown in Figure 5(a), we
796	find that the data curriculum (Ascend+WSD) may only achieve a marginal improvement or even
797	fail to match the performance of uniform ordering (Uniform+WSD) when the ending LR is close to
798	zero, like at the scale of 10−5. However, as the ending LR increases, the performance of curriculum
799	training improves, but may degrade when the ending LR approaches the peak LR. Note that the

1030	Mid-training is an emerging practice in

1035	data. The CMA results (e.g., EMA + A-T) show a significant advantage over the WSD schedule

1038	additional complex data filtering is applied. A possible explanation for the more prominent im-
1039	provement is that, when high-quality data is sparse, each sample provides a relatively more valuable
1040	signal for parameter updates, amplifying the benefit of CMA.

1042	In practice, sorting an entire data cor-
1043	pus globally may not be feasible. As an alternative, we tested a strategy where data is sorted in
1044	ascending order within each training phase separately (A,A in Table 2). The results show that the
1045	benefits of our approach over standard LR decay largely persist. However, applying a curriculum
1046	only to the final, high-quality data phase (EMA + U,A) is not sufficient for optimal results. The su-
1047	perior performance of the A,A schedule over U,A suggests that applying a curriculum to the initial,
1048	lower-quality data phase is also beneficial. One possible explanation is that reordering data in the
1049	lower-quality phase can exploit the model’s forgetting mechanism to mitigate the adverse effects of
1050	toxic samples that pass through the cleaning pipeline by chance. These results further confirm the
1051	synergy between model averaging and a data curriculum.

Strategic Data Ordering: Enhancing Large Language Model Performance
through Curriculum Learning
Jisu Kim
Diqest
jisukim8873@gmail.com
Juhwan Lee
Diqest
9521ljh@gmail.com
Abstract
The rapid advancement of Large Language
Models (LLMs) has improved text understand-
ing and generation but poses challenges in com-
putational resources. This study proposes a cur-
riculum learning-inspired, data-centric training
strategy that begins with simpler tasks and pro-
gresses to more complex ones, using criteria
such as prompt length, attention scores, and
loss values to structure the training data. Ex-
periments with Mistral-7B (Jiang et al., 2023)
and Gemma-7B (Team et al., 2024) models
demonstrate that curriculum learning slightly
improves performance compared to traditional
random data shuffling. Notably, we observed
that sorting data based on our proposed atten-
tion criteria generally led to better performance.
This approach offers a sustainable method to
enhance LLM performance without increasing
model size or dataset volume, addressing scala-
bility challenges in LLM training.
1
Introduction
The rapid advancement of Large Language Models
(LLMs) has been a defining trend in artificial intelli-
gence, reshaping the capabilities of machines in un-
derstanding and generating human-like text. This
surge in progress can be traced back to the intro-
duction of the Transformer architecture (Vaswani
et al., 2017), which laid the groundwork for the
development of models such as the Generative Pre-
trained Transformer (GPT) family. These models
have been pivotal in pushing the boundaries of what
machines can achieve, largely due to their expan-
sive parameter counts and sophisticated training
methodologies. The Transformer’s introduction
has not only catalyzed significant progress but also
sparked a paradigm shift in how we approach ma-
chine learning tasks (Acheampong et al., 2021; Pat-
wardhan et al., 2023; Ali et al., 2024).
OpenAI’s research underscores a key observa-
tion in the progression of these models: larger mod-
els tend to exhibit superior performance (Kaplan
et al., 2020). However, this approach of scaling up
models introduces a set of challenges, notably the
increased demand for computational resources and
associated costs. As the size of models escalates, it
prompts a crucial question about the sustainability
of such growth trajectories and whether alternative
strategies might offer more efficient pathways to
improving model performance.
In response to these challenges, we proposes a
data-centric training strategy, inspired by the ped-
agogical concept of curriculum learning. Curricu-
lum learning, a strategy that mimics human edu-
cational approaches by starting with simpler tasks
and progressively moving to more complex ones.
By structuring the training data and tasks in a man-
ner that reflects the incremental learning stages
humans go through, this method aims to facilitate a
more natural and efficient learning process for the
models. This approach deviates from traditional
training practices, which often involve exposing
models to a random assortment of data, suggesting
a structured progression could yield better perfor-
mance and efficiency.
The potential of curriculum learning in the realm
of LLMs is profound. It not only aligns with cog-
nitive and educational theories but also presents a
practical framework to tackle the scalability chal-
lenges associated with model training. By focusing
on the complexity of training data and adopting a
gradual learning, curriculum learning could lead
to the better performance without the necessity for
constant increases in model size.
Therefore, we focuses on data-centric strategy
training method by curriculumn learning, by exam-
ining the impact of performance of model, compar-
ing random shuffled training dataset.
This study focuses on a data-centric strategy to
enhance model performance through the adoption
of curriculum learning. By examining the impact of
structured training data, this study aims to demon-
strate its effectiveness relative to the traditional
arXiv:2405.07490v1  [cs.CL]  13 May 2024

method of random shuffling. We seek to establish
that curriculum learning is a crucial strategy for im-
proving the development process of large language
models, potentially achieving better performance
without increasing the model parameters or the size
of the dataset.
2
Related Work
Curriculum learning, introduced by Bengio et al.
in 2009 (Bengio et al., 2009), is a learning strat-
egy where models are trained on data from simple
to complex, mirroring human learning processes.
This approach enhances model performance by es-
tablishing a foundational understanding before in-
troducing more complex data. It has been widely
applied in natural language processing (NLP) and
computer vision. (Guo et al., 2018; Antonios Pla-
tanios et al., 2019; Tay et al., 2019).
In NLP, curriculum learning has proven to be
effective by organizing the training sequence to
begin with simpler texts and progressively transi-
tion to more complex ones. The complexity of
these texts is assessed based on various criteria,
including text length, the rarity of vocabulary, and
edit distance. This structured approach has suc-
cessfully demonstrated the efficacy of curriculum
learning in the training of Pretrained Language
Models (PLMs) (Chang et al., 2021; Nagatsuka
et al., 2023).
Recent advancements in large-scale language
and multimodal models have highlighted the ef-
fective integration of curriculum learning with
cutting-edge techniques, significantly boosting per-
formance across various applications.
Notably,
projects such as WavLLM (Hu et al., 2024) and
AutoWebGLM (Lai et al., 2024) showcase the po-
tential of these integrations, tailoring the learning
process to gradually introduce more complex tasks,
thereby enhancing model robustness and applica-
tion specificity. Alongside these innovations, fur-
ther research has validated the effectiveness of cur-
riculum learning in instruction tuning for language
models. This approach not only systematically im-
proves models’ abilities to handle progressively
challenging tasks but also optimizes their learn-
ing trajectory for better performance in specialized
tasks. By methodically structuring the training pro-
cess, these initiatives have set a new standard in the
development and refinement of AI models, marking
a significant step forward in their evolution.
In the development of training data for curricu-
lum learning, accurately measuring data difficulty
is crucial. Specifically, for LLMs (Large Language
Models), determining the degree of data difficulty
is challenging. Traditional metrics, such as text
length or word rarity, are often employed to esti-
mate the difficulty of training data (Chang et al.,
2021; Nagatsuka et al., 2023). However, these
metrics may not fully reflect the complexity of a
dataset. It is essential to assess data difficulty from
the model’s perspective, rather than relying solely
on data-specific metrics. Our research proposes a
new approach to calculate the degree of difficulty
based on a model-centric perspective. By organiz-
ing the training dataset according to difficulty using
our new metric, we aim to improve the model’s per-
formance compared to random shuffling.
3
Methods for Quantitative Difficulty
Measurement
In this section, we introduce a novel methodology
for training models that begins with easier tasks
and methodically progresses to more challenging
ones. This approach requires organizing data by its
level of complexity, for which we have established
three principal criteria. By arranging the data in
an order that goes from less to more difficult, this
approach establishes a structured progression for
learning.
Length
It is widely acknowledged in the study that longer
sentences are more challenging to learn. To assess
difficulty based on length, we address the measure-
ment of length in tokenized prompt, a critical factor
in understanding the complexities of language pro-
cessing. The prompt length, denoted as dlength(p),
is defined as the total number of tokens produced by
the tokenizer for a given prompt. Mathematically,
it is represented as:
dlength(p) = N.

Attention Score
We introduce a novel method to determine the
complexity of a prompt by analyzing model at-
tention scores.
In our approach, we suggest
that how a model focuses on different parts of a
prompt—reflected by attention scores—can show
how difficult the prompt is. If a model concentrates
its attention on just a few token parts, the prompt
is likely easier since only those parts are needed to
find the answer. However, if the attention is spread

evenly across the whole prompt, it’s harder, indicat-
ing that understanding everything is necessary to
get the right answer. We measure this by looking at
the variation in attention scores, using two specific
methods.
This study focus exclusively on the attention
scores for tokens following the section where the
response is generated to analyze response genera-
tion. We calculate the variance of attention scores
within each attention layer for these tokens and
then average these variances across all layers. This
process is mathematically represented as:
1. For each layer i, calculate the variance of at-
tention scores, Var(Ai), for tokens after the
section where the response is generated.
2. Compute the average variance across all N

Loss
A high loss signifies a substantial discrepancy be-
tween the predicted and actual outcomes, indicat-
ing that the model perceives the data as challenging.
We establish a direct correlation between high loss
values and increased difficulty. Therefore, prompts
that generate higher loss are considered more chal-

4
Experiment Settings
Models
In order to validate our hypotheses, this study con-
ducted a series of experiments utilizing language
models with 7 billion parameters. Specifically, we
utilized the Mistral-7B and Gemma-7B models to
conduct our analyses (Jiang et al., 2023; Team
et al., 2024).
In addition,
because of limited resources,
we utilized Quantize Low Rank Approximation
(QLoRA) (Hu et al., 2021) with Parameter-Efficient
Fine-Tuning (PEFT) library to fine-tune the mod-
els. Different from full fine-tuning, LoRA freezes
the pre-trained model weights and injects learnable
rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the
Transformer architecture. Thus, this method can
reduce the number of trainable parameters, the cost
of training and time for downstream tasks. The
details of configurations are described on Table 1.
Instruction tuning Datasets
This study focus on specific datasets that are con-
sidered the state-of-art results for instruction tun-
ing. Due to the memory limitations of our hard-
ware setup, this study is limited to using single-turn
datasets.
• Orca-math (Mitra et al., 2024) This dataset
contains answers generated for elementary
school math word problems using Azure GPT-
4 Turbo.
• Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023) This dataset was
created using the Self-Instruct (Wang et al.,
2022) method and the OpenAI Text-Davinci-
003 model.
• SlimOrca-Dedup (Lian et al., 2023b) This is
a subset of the OpenOrca (Mukherjee et al.,
2023) data, where, within the FLAN (Longpre
et al., 2023) dataset, incorrect answers were
identified and removed using OpenAI GPT-4
based on human annotations, and duplicates
were eliminated in the SlimOrca (Lian et al.,
2023a) dataset.
5
Evaluation
Language Model Evaluation Harness
In order to evaluate instruction-tuned model, we
used Language Model Evaluation Harness (Gao
et al., 2023) a framework for few-shot evaluation
of language models. This method conducted ARC
with 25 shot (Clark et al., 2018), HellaSwag with
10 shots (Zellers et al., 2019), MMLU with 5
shot (Hendrycks et al., 2021), TrustfulQA with a 0
shot (Lin et al., 2021), Winogrande with 5 shot (ai2,
2019) and GSM8K with 5 shot (Cobbe et al., 2021)
datasets. The combination of these datasets ex-
tensively evaluates the ability of Large Language
Models to respond to realistic questions and rea-
soning. By evaluating these datasets, we verify
whether our proposed curriculum learning method
impacts the model outcomes.

Results
Random Sorting in First Epoch with
Subsequent Difficulty-Based Curriculum
Learning
To enhance the efficiency of training, we cus-
tomized the HuggingFace Trainer to perform in-
struction tuning randomly during the initial epoch.
From the second epoch, we systematically arranged
the data to align with specific methods for instruc-
tion tuning. This approach was designed to assess
the impact of structured versus random data pre-
sentation on the model’s learning dynamics and
overall performance.
In case of Mistral-7B, as shown in Table 2,
instruction-tuning on the alpaca dataset did not
yield performance improvements over the origi-
nal model configuration. When comparing vari-
ous instruction-tuning strategies, the most effec-
tive approach involved random data arrangement
trained for only one epoch, achieving an accuracy
of 60.91%.
However, experiments conducted on the Orca-
math dataset revealed that the most effective strat-
egy involved aligning data based on attention mech-
anisms with three epochs. This approach resulted
in the highest mean accuracy of 66.28% as shown
in Table 3.
When experimenting with the Slimorca dataset,
the most effective training strategy involved or-
ganizing the data based on sequence length and
limiting the training to two epochs. This method
achieved the best performance with an accuracy of
65.08% (Table 4).
For the Gemma-7B model, experiments con-
ducted using the Alpaca dataset indicated that ran-
dom data arrangement during instruction-tuning
yielded the highest average performance, achieving
an accuracy of 64.10% (Tabel 5).
Conversely, results from Table 6 and 7, con-
ducted on the orca-math and slimorca-dedup
datasets, indicate that attention-based curriculum
learning was most effective. Specifically, in the
orcamath dataset, this method achieved the best
performance with an accuracy of 67.54% after two
epochs of training. Similarly, for the slimorca-
dedup dataset, curriculum learning based on atten-
tion mechanisms and extending training to three
epochs yielded the highest accuracy of 66.87%.
7
Conclusion and Future Works
While our proposed attention-based method has
shown a tendency to improve instruction tuning,
the differences observed have not been significantly
impactful. Consequently, we plan to upload the
results evaluated using the alpacaeval dataset in
version 2 of our project. Currently, our instruction
tuning approach involves random training for the
first epoch, followed by structured data training
in subsequent epochs. Therefore, the results are
heavily reliant on the outcomes from the randomly
trained model. In the next version, we intend to
prepare a pre-arranged dataset and begin the train-
ing from the first epoch with this structured data to
better assess the effectiveness of this approach.

Here is a comprehensive summary of the paper and its relevance to how data ordering/curriculum affects LLM pretraining and generalization.

---

## Skill-it! (Chen et al., 2023) -- Summary

**Authors:** Mayee F. Chen, Nicholas Roberts, Kush Bhatia, Jue Wang, Ce Zhang, Frederic Sala, Christopher Re (Stanford, UW-Madison, Together AI, U Chicago)

**Paper:** arXiv 2307.14430

**Code:** No explicit code link is provided in the main paper text. The acknowledgements mention Together Computer for compute resources.

---

### Definition of "Skills"

The paper introduces two formal definitions:

1. **Skill (Definition 2.1):** A skill `s` is a unit of behavior with associated data `X_s` such that if a model `f` is trained on a dataset `D_s` drawn from `X_s`, then `f` shows improved metric (e.g., lower cross-entropy validation loss) on held-out samples from `X_s`. This is intentionally flexible -- a skill can be a granular task (e.g., "Spanish question generation") or a broad data source (e.g., "legal text from tax court rulings").

2. **Ordered Skill Set (Definition 2.2):** A collection of skills with a directed **skills graph** `G = (S, E)` that is neither complete nor empty. An edge `(s_i, s_j)` exists if the amount of data needed to learn `s_j` when training on both `D_{s_i}` and `D_{s_j}` is less than when training only on `D_{s_j}`. This captures prerequisite relationships among skills.

The key insight is that not just any semantic grouping of data produces a useful ordered skill set. The authors tested instruction types on Alpaca (yielded a nearly complete graph, 97.4% dense -- no benefit from skill-based sampling), data sources on Pile of Law (nearly empty graph, 3.9% dense -- skills are independent), and task categories on Natural Instructions (intermediate density, 42.7% -- the sweet spot where skill ordering helps).

---

### Curriculum Learning Approach Based on Skill Dependencies

The paper proposes two methods that exploit the skills graph:

1. **Skill-stratified sampling:** A static method that uniformly samples from a target skill and its identified prerequisite skills. Simple but does not adapt during training.

2. **SKILL-IT (the main contribution):** An online data selection algorithm derived from online mirror descent. At each round `t`:
   - Observe validation losses on evaluation skills
   - Update the sampling mixture using: `p^i_{t+1} = exp(eta * sum over window of sum_j A_{ij} * L_{eval,j}(f_tau))`
   - This allocates more weight to (a) prerequisite skills that influence unlearned evaluation skills, and (b) skills that still have high validation loss

   The algorithm uses a learned **skills graph adjacency matrix** `A` where `A_{ij}` captures the strength of influence from training skill `i` to evaluation skill `j`. The graph can be learned via brute-force (O(Hk^2)) or a linear approximation (O(hk)), and graphs learned on smaller models transfer to larger models.

The framework operates in three settings:
- **Continual pre-training:** S_eval = S_train (learn all skills)
- **Fine-tuning:** S_eval is a subset of S_train (learn a target skill)
- **Out-of-domain:** S_eval and S_train are disjoint (generalize to unseen evaluation skills)

---

### Datasets Used

1. **LEGO synthetic** (from Zhang et al., 2022): Tests chain-of-reasoning ability. Variables with binary labels linked by assertion/negation chains. Skills defined by reasoning chain depth (k=5). Used for continual pre-training and fine-tuning experiments.

2. **Addition synthetic** (variant of Nanda et al., 2023): 3-digit addition where each digit prediction is a skill. Demonstrates that even the ones digit skill benefits from simultaneously learning tens digit -- models do not necessarily learn digits in the "obvious" order.

3. **Natural Instructions (NI)** (Wang et al., 2022): Real NLP dataset with 1600+ tasks. Skills defined as task categories (23 for training, 12 for test evaluation in the out-of-domain setting). Used across all three settings.

4. **RedPajama** (Together, 2023): 1.2 trillion token dataset. Data sources (ArXiv, Books, C4, CommonCrawl, GitHub, StackExchange, Wikipedia) treated as training skills. Evaluation skills from the LM Evaluation Harness. Used for a 3B parameter continual pre-training case study.

5. **Alpaca** (negative result): Instruction types as skills yielded a nearly complete graph -- skill-based sampling did not help.

6. **Pile of Law** (negative result): Data sources as skills yielded a nearly empty graph -- skills were independent.

---

### Key Results

**Continual pre-training:**
- LEGO: SKILL-IT achieves 36.5 points higher accuracy than random sampling; 35.8 points over both random and curriculum learning. Random/curriculum/anticurriculum all plateau on 4 of 5 skills, while SKILL-IT learns all 5.
- Addition: SKILL-IT converges to near-zero loss faster; random sampling fails to learn skill 1 (ones digit).
- NI: 3.2% lower validation loss than random sampling.

**Fine-tuning:**
- LEGO skill 3: Same validation loss in 38.1% fewer steps than training on target skill only.
- Addition skill 1: Converges in 59% fewer steps.
- NI Spanish QG: 5.3% lower validation loss (using only 25% of the Spanish QG data that the baseline uses).
- NI Stance Detection: 13.6% lower validation loss than training on stance detection alone.

**Out-of-domain:**
- NI test tasks: SKILL-IT achieves lowest loss on 11 out of 12 evaluation task categories over random and skill-stratified sampling.

**RedPajama (3B parameter model):**
- SKILL-IT achieves higher accuracy on the LM Evaluation Harness with 1B additional tokens than uniform sampling with 3B additional tokens -- a 3x data efficiency improvement. The learned mixture heavily weights C4 (42%), GitHub (19%), and ArXiv (14%).

**Skill recovery:** Embedding-based clustering fails to recover skills (below 39% accuracy on LEGO). Loss-trajectory-based clustering (clustering by per-sample loss across 10 training runs) achieves 61% accuracy.

---

### Relevance to Data Ordering/Curriculum for LLM Pretraining and Generalization

This paper provides several key insights for the distribution shift curriculum research question:

1. **Prerequisite structure matters more than easy-to-hard ordering.** Traditional curriculum learning (Bengio et al., 2009) orders individual samples from easy to hard, but SKILL-IT operates on a skills graph that captures dependency structure. The paper shows that standard curriculum and anticurriculum learning both fail on LEGO (plateauing on most skills), while graph-aware ordering succeeds. This suggests that for domain generalization, understanding which data sources are prerequisites for others is more important than sample-level difficulty ordering.

2. **Training on mixtures of prerequisite skills is more data-efficient than training on the target skill alone.** Spanish QG is learned more efficiently when the model also trains on English QG, Spanish QA, and English QA -- using only 25% of the Spanish QG data. This has direct implications for domain adaptation: to generalize to a new domain, one should identify and train on prerequisite skills rather than just collecting more target-domain data.

3. **Dynamic reweighting outperforms static mixtures.** SKILL-IT's online adjustment of sampling weights -- allocating more weight to unlearned skills and their prerequisites as training progresses -- consistently outperforms static skill-stratified sampling. This suggests that curriculum strategies for pretraining should be adaptive.

4. **Skills graphs transfer across model scales.** The paper notes (Appendix D.4) that skills graphs learned on 125M parameter models can be used for data selection on 1.3B parameter models, making the approach practical for large-scale pretraining.

5. **The 3x data efficiency result on RedPajama** (1B tokens with SKILL-IT matching 3B tokens with uniform sampling) demonstrates that skill-aware data ordering can yield substantial compute savings at pretraining scale, directly relevant to efficient LLM training under distribution shift.

6. **Not all data groupings are useful.** The paper's negative results (Alpaca instruction types, Pile of Law sources) show that the choice of how to define skills is critical -- the grouping must produce an intermediate-density graph to benefit from ordering.

Samples with high learnability are those the proxy model found most learnable (largest loss decrease during training). These are prioritized in the curriculum.

1. Train a small proxy model on a holdout set, saving an early checkpoint (at step t0) and a late checkpoint (at step T). The late-stage loss is averaged over the last three checkpoints.

## Summary: "Strategic Data Ordering: Enhancing Large Language Model Performance through Curriculum Learning" (Kim & Lee, 2024)

### Methodology for Data Ordering

The paper applies curriculum learning to LLM instruction tuning by ordering training data from easy to hard. The training protocol uses **random ordering for the first epoch**, then switches to difficulty-based ordering for subsequent epochs (epochs 2 and 3). This was implemented by customizing the HuggingFace Trainer. The authors acknowledge this is a limitation -- the results are "heavily reliant on the outcomes from the randomly trained model" -- and note plans to start structured ordering from epoch 1 in future work.

### Difficulty/Ordering Criteria (Three Criteria Proposed)

1. **Prompt Length** (`d_length`): Simply the number of tokens in the tokenized prompt. Longer prompts are considered harder. This is a traditional, data-centric metric.

2. **Attention Score** (novel, model-centric metric): They analyze the variance of attention scores across layers for response-generation tokens. The intuition: if model attention is concentrated on a few tokens, the prompt is easier (only a few parts needed to find the answer). If attention is spread evenly (low variance), the prompt is harder (understanding everything is necessary). They compute variance of attention scores within each layer, then average across all N layers.

3. **Loss**: Cross-entropy loss on the answer segment. Higher loss = the model finds the data more challenging. This is also a model-centric metric.

The attention-based criterion is the paper's primary novel contribution, framing difficulty from the model's perspective rather than relying solely on surface-level text features.

### Datasets and Model Architectures

**Models (both 7B parameters):**
- Mistral-7B
- Gemma-7B
- Fine-tuned using QLoRA (rank=64, alpha=16, dropout=0.1) with PEFT, targeting q/k/v/o/gate/up/down projection layers

**Instruction-tuning datasets (all single-turn):**
- **Orca-math**: Elementary school math word problems with GPT-4 Turbo generated answers
- **Alpaca**: Self-Instruct method with OpenAI Text-Davinci-003
- **SlimOrca-Dedup**: Cleaned subset of OpenOrca/FLAN, with GPT-4-verified removal of incorrect answers and deduplication

**Evaluation benchmarks** (via LM Evaluation Harness):
- ARC (25-shot), HellaSwag (10-shot), MMLU (5-shot), TruthfulQA (0-shot), Winogrande (5-shot), GSM8K (5-shot)

### Key Results on Whether Strategic Ordering Helps

The results are **mixed and the improvements are modest**:

**Mistral-7B:**
- **Alpaca**: Curriculum learning did NOT help. Random 1-epoch (60.91%) beat all curriculum variants. Even the base model (60.99%) outperformed most fine-tuned versions.
- **Orca-math**: Attention-based ordering at 3 epochs achieved the best result (66.28%), slightly above random at 2 epochs (66.16%).
- **SlimOrca-Dedup**: Length-based ordering at 2 epochs was best (65.08%), slightly above random at 1 epoch (65.04%).

**Gemma-7B:**
- **Alpaca**: Random ordering was best (64.10%). Curriculum learning did not help.
- **Orca-math**: Attention-based ordering at 2 epochs was best (67.54%), above random at 2 epochs (66.95%).
- **SlimOrca-Dedup**: Attention-based ordering at 3 epochs was best (66.87%), above random at 2 epochs (66.50%).

**Overall pattern**: Attention-based curriculum learning "generally led to better performance," particularly on the Orca-math and SlimOrca-Dedup datasets, but the authors explicitly acknowledge that "the differences observed have not been significantly impactful." The gains are typically in the range of 0.1-0.6 percentage points over random ordering. Loss-based ordering tended to perform worst among the curriculum methods.

### Findings about Generalization to New Distributions

The paper does **not directly study generalization to new or shifted distributions**. The evaluation is on standard benchmarks (ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, Winogrande, GSM8K) which test general capabilities rather than distribution shift robustness. There are no experiments explicitly measuring out-of-distribution generalization, domain transfer, or robustness to distribution shifts. The paper frames its contribution purely in terms of improving training efficiency and benchmark performance within the standard instruction-tuning paradigm.

### Key Limitations and Caveats
- Random ordering is used for the first epoch in all curriculum conditions, confounding the effect of data ordering
- Only QLoRA fine-tuning (not full fine-tuning) was tested
- Only single-turn datasets due to hardware constraints
- No statistical significance testing is reported for the small differences observed
- The authors themselves characterize the improvements as not "significantly impactful"
